strengths: The paper addresses a clear clinical NLP data-access problem with 8,767 synthetic examples spanning 15 annotated categories, with text spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. The reported release of the dataset, expert-corrected test set, and checkpoints offers practical research value.

Real-data experiments provide convincing evidence of classification utility. Prompt-based RoBERTa improves MIMIC-SBDH macro-F from 55.64 to 91.11, while standard RoBERTa improves VA-SBDH macro-F from 72.38 to 80.71. Multiple architectures, three independent runs, and training-size analyses strengthen this evidence.

Two experienced annotators reviewed the entire 1,755-example synthetic test set, adjudicated disagreements, corrected rationales, and added missing annotations. The detailed error analysis usefully exposes limitations of GPT-4-generated supervision.

The appendices document generation prompts, all 45 seed examples, category definitions, task transformations, and training configurations. The resource and demonstrated classification improvements support a Findings recommendation.
weaknesses: The headline claim of consistent improvement is broader than the results support. RoBERTa’s VA NER macro-F decreases slightly, and several Mamba and Llama settings show negligible or negative gains. The large T5 NER improvement starts from an exceptionally unstable baseline, while the 94.44-point housing-insecurity gain involves only 18 positive test examples. Variation across three training runs does not capture uncertainty from this small test sample.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the benefits of synthetic supervision from additional training and class balancing. MLC receives 40 extra synthetic-training epochs, without clearly reported compute-matched target-only or rebalanced baselines. Appendix D.2 describes a real-data pretraining control, but Table 13 does not distinguish that condition from the target-only baseline despite serving both comparisons.

The expert-reviewed benchmark is partly dependent on GPT-4’s proposed annotations. Appendix E.2 accepts an overlapping category when GPT-4 selected it, but prioritizes a more specific category when humans add an annotation. This can produce inconsistent reference labels. Furthermore, the 71.06% human–LLM alignment includes newly added annotations in its denominator, whereas LLM self-evaluation excludes missing annotations; these agreement figures are not directly comparable.

The reasoning-distillation claim remains weakly supported. DSS improves macro-F by only 0.66 points for T5 and 0.58 for FLAN-T5-base, with the latter statistically nonsignificant (p=0.36). Evaluation is confined to synthetic text, and extraction accuracy alone does not establish transferred reasoning ability. Real-data extraction evaluation after DSS pretraining would not require rationale annotations at evaluation time.

The resource’s clinical coverage is narrower than its benchmark framing suggests. Examples average 13.7 words, versus 35.13 and 47.43 in the real datasets. Experiments retain positive annotations and do not directly evaluate temporal prediction or negation handling. The transfer results demonstrate usefulness after target-domain supervision, with limited evidence about performance on unseen clinical settings.

Some reproducibility details need correction or clarification: the stated synthetic split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767, and the ROUGE-L filtering rule ambiguously requires similarity to 'all' previous examples rather than any matching example. Exact prompt-based classification templates and patient-level split safeguards are not clearly documented. The private VA dataset also limits independent replication of the real-data NER results.
